## Three Desk Failures {.center}

A forecast that was **too confident**.

. . .

A portfolio that looked **diversified** — and wasn't.

. . .

A model declared **fair** — that wasn't.

. . .

All three are the *same* mistake about one thing: **dependence**.

## One Noun, Three Verbs {.center}

This course turns on a single idea — **dependence** — and the three things you
ever do with it:

. . .

* **measure** it
* **remove** the part you may not keep
* **propagate** it honestly

. . .

…and one operation underneath all three: a **change of variables**.

## Failure 1 — The Over-Confident Forecast

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
grid = np.linspace(-8, 8, 600)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
ax.fill_between(grid, norm.pdf(grid, 0, 1), color=WARM, alpha=0.35,
                label="what the model claimed")
ax.plot(grid, student_t.pdf(grid, df=2.5), c=INK, lw=2.2,
        label="what actually happened")
ax.axvline(-4.6, color=CRASH, lw=2, label="the loss")
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("return")
ax.legend(fontsize=11, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A point forecast — or a thin Gaussian band — hides the loss in the tail it never
represented. *(Module 3.)*

## Failure 2 — "Diversified," Then a Co-Crash

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.8
a, b, crash = datasets.two_banks(n=600)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8))
ax.scatter(a[~crash], b[~crash], s=12, c=COOL, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
ax.scatter(a[crash], b[crash], s=24, c=CRASH, alpha=0.9, edgecolors="none",
           label="they fall together")
ax.set_title(f"Pearson r = {pearsonr(a, b)[0]:+.2f} — but look at the corner",
             fontsize=12)
ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.legend(fontsize=11, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Low average correlation, yet they crash **together**. Correlation only sees
straight lines. *(Modules 1–2.)*

## Failure 3 — "Fair" Because It Ignores the Attribute

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.4
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 700
S = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
score = (S**2 - 1) + 0.4 * rng.normal(0, 1, n)
bins = np.linspace(S.min(), S.max(), 11); idx = np.digitize(S, bins)
ctr = 0.5 * (bins[:-1] + bins[1:])
mean = [score[idx == k].mean() for k in range(1, len(bins))]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.4))
ax.scatter(S, score, s=10, c=COOL, alpha=0.2, edgecolors="none")
ax.plot(ctr, mean, "-o", c=CRASH, lw=2.4, label="mean score bends with S")
ax.set_title(f"Pearson ≈ {pearsonr(score, S)[0]:+.2f}  →  'neutral'", fontsize=12)
ax.set_xlabel("protected attribute S"); ax.set_ylabel("model score")
ax.legend(fontsize=11, frameon=False); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The score never used $S$, yet it tracks it — through proxies, in a curve
correlation can't see. *(Module 4.)*

## The Axiom {.center}

> **Claim only what your evidence justifies.**

. . .

The least-committal distribution for what you know is the most honest one — and
the **Gaussian** is the least-committal joint of all.

. . .

So *what we add to or remove from a Gaussian is exactly the dependence in the
data.*

## The Through-Line

| Module | Verb | Question |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · Dependence | **measure** | how much do two things move together? |
| 2 · Gaussianization | (the engine) | turn messy data Gaussian, invertibly |
| 3 · Uncertainty | **propagate** | carry risk forward without losing the tail |
| 4 · Fair learning | **remove** | make a model blind to a chosen variable |

. . .

The same change-of-variables map runs **forward** to measure and remove,
**backward** to propagate.

## The Ideal vs. the Shortcut {.center}

That one invertible map is the **clean picture** — the exact way to see all four
verbs as one operation.

. . .

But an exact map is expensive.

. . .

So in practice each module **trades exactness for a cheaper estimator** that
measures the same dependence a different way.

## The Shortcut, Module by Module

| Module | The exact map | The practical shortcut |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · measure | MI via gaussianization | histogram MI, correlation, CKA |
| 3 · propagate | invert $T$, draw scenarios | ensembles, predict-the-noise |
| 4 · remove | conditional transform | a **penalty** in the loss |

. . .

So the spine is the *ideal*; much of the course is learning **when the shortcut
is good enough — and when only the exact map will do.**
